docs.title: Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon
docs.text:
Six standalone, fully tested implementations — one per prize category — for the Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon, plus the research behind them and the tooling used to ship and demo them.

:octicons-mark-github-16: View the repo Devpost submission draft

docs.title: Prize categories
docs.text:
Category Project Track prize Alexa+ HomeOps — household operations MCP server $25,000 top prize Fire TV CourtSide — AI co-commentator backend $25,000 top prize Ring PorchPass — delegated access control $12,000 top prize Bee StudyLoop — ambient study session coach $12,000 top prize AWS Builder (mini) Model Router — SageMaker sidecar pattern $5,000 Open Source (mini) friction-log-toolkit — friction-log CLI $5,000

A project can win at most one track prize plus one mini-challenge prize — see the Devpost submission draft for the recommended pairing and per-project write-ups.

docs.title: What's real here
docs.text: Every project is genuinely working code, not a mockup: real HTTP/MCP end-to-end tests, real protocol implementations (MCP elicitation, sampling, resumable transport; HMAC-signed webhooks; Server-Sent Events; a real SM-2 spaced-repetition scheduler), and an honest interface boundary wherever real hardware or credentials weren't available in the build environment (Ring, Bee, Fire TV, Bedrock, SageMaker) — each documented in that project's own README as the exact seam where the real integration plugs in.

docs.title: Demo video narration (Amazon Polly)
docs.text: narration.ssml is the voiceover script for the Devpost demo video, sized to run well under the hackathon's 3-minute cap (~313 words plus pauses — roughly 2:00–2:30 spoken by Polly, leaving room for a silent title card and closing card). It covers the recommended primary submission from ../DEVPOST_SUBMISSION.md: HomeOps (Alexa+ track) plus the friction-log-toolkit (Open Source mini-challenge).

docs.title: Rendering it with Polly
docs.text:
Requires the AWS CLI configured with Polly access (works from AWS CloudShell with no extra setup, same as ../deploy/).

# Audio only, neural voice (Matthew or Joanna both work well for this tone):
aws polly synthesize-speech \
  --engine neural \
  --voice-id Matthew \
  --text-type ssml \
  --text file://demo/narration.ssml \
  --output-format mp3 \
  demo/narration.mp3

docs.title: Getting timing marks (to sync screen recording cuts)
docs.text:
Every section of the script has a <mark name="..."/> at the point where the screen recording should cut to the next feature. Polly can return the exact millisecond offset of each mark, so you can cut your screen capture to match the narration instead of eyeballing it:

aws polly synthesize-speech \
  --engine neural \
  --voice-id Matthew \
  --text-type ssml \
  --text file://demo/narration.ssml \
  --output-format json \
  --speech-mark-types '["ssml"]' \
  demo/narration-marks.json

narration-marks.json will contain one JSON line per mark, each with a time field in milliseconds from the start of narration.mp3 — cut your screen recording to the next shot the instant that mark's timestamp passes.

docs.title: Shot list (matches each <mark>)
docs.text: Mark What's being said What to show on screen intro_start The one-command-at-a-time problem, then HomeOps's pitch Title card, or Alexa+ device idle feature_tasks Adding a task with fair auto-assignment Terminal/client calling add_task, showing the assignee it picked feature_reorder Elicitation-gated reorder reorder_item triggering a real elicitation prompt the user approves feature_budget Budget alert + generate_weekly_narrative via sampling An expense pushing a category over budget, then the generated narrative text appearing feature_briefing The run_morning_briefing compound tool One call to run_morning_briefing, then the combined tasks/budget/stock narration it returns opensource_start friction-log-toolkit pitch friction-log add "..." --tag friction in a terminal, then friction-log export producing the Markdown report close_start Closing line Repo README or the six-project folder listing

docs.title: Notes on the SSML
docs.text:
• Wrapped in <amazon:domain name="conversational"> for a natural, non-robotic delivery — supported by Polly's neural engine on voices like Matthew, Joanna, and Matthew-Neural equivalents in other locales.
  • MCP, API, and similar acronyms use <say-as interpret-as="characters"> so Polly spells them out (M-C-P) instead of trying to pronounce them as a word.
  • Only SSML tags supported by Polly's neural engine are used (speak, amazon:domain, break, emphasis, say-as, mark) — no <prosody pitch> or <amazon:effect name="whispered">, which neural voices don't support.
  • If you'd rather use the standard (non-neural) engine, drop --engine neural — the script is compatible with both, though amazon:domain sounds best on neural voices.

docs.title: Deploying to AWS from CloudShell
docs.text: Scripts to deploy any of this repo's five backend services to a live, public HTTPS endpoint using only AWS CloudShell — no local machine setup required.

docs.title: Why Amazon ECS Express Mode (not App Runner)
docs.text:
These scripts originally targeted AWS App Runner. AWS closed App Runner to new customers on April 30, 2026 — existing App Runner customers are unaffected, but a fresh AWS account (the common case for a hackathon judge or a new team) cannot create its first App Runner service anymore. AWS's own documented successor is Amazon ECS Express Mode (GA at re:Invent 2025), which preserves the same pitch — one CLI call, a container image plus two IAM roles, and ECS provisions a Fargate service, an Application Load Balancer, auto scaling, and a live HTTPS endpoint — while running on the regular ECS control plane instead of a separate product. These scripts were rewritten to target it.

It's also still the right fit technically for the same reason App Runner was: several of these services (PorchPass's live event feed, CourtSide's live commentary stream, the model router's streamed classification endpoint) hold long-lived Server-Sent-Events connections, which don't survive Lambda + API Gateway's request/response model. Express Mode just runs the same Express server these apps already run locally — nothing about the app code changes for deployment.

friction-log-toolkit is not deployed by these scripts — it's a CLI tool, not a server, so there's nothing to run behind a URL. See its own README for installation instead.

A note on how new this is: ECS Express Mode is a very new AWS API surface, and its exact CLI response shape wasn't consistently documented everywhere at the time these scripts were written. deploy.sh extracts the service URL defensively (scanning the response for any field that looks like a URL, rather than assuming one exact key name) and always prints where to find the real service in the AWS Console as a fallback. If the AWS CLI's behavior has since diverged from what's here, aws ecs create-express-gateway-service help is the source of truth — please open an issue/PR if you hit a mismatch.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An AWS account and credentials available in your shell. In AWS CloudShell, this is automatic — just open a CloudShell tab in the AWS Console for the account/region you want to deploy into.
  • The IAM identity CloudShell is using needs permission to manage ECR repositories, ECS (including create-express-gateway-service/delete-express-gateway-service), and (once, the first time you deploy anything) create two IAM roles. AdministratorAccess, or a policy covering ecr:*, ecs:*, and iam:CreateRole/GetRole/AttachRolePolicy, is enough.
  • Docker, jq, and the AWS CLI v2 are all preinstalled in CloudShell — nothing else to install. (jq is used only to make reading the deploy response nicer; the scripts fall back to plain grep if it's ever missing.)

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/<your-fork>/Build-Ship-Shape-Amazon-Developer-Hackathon.git
cd Build-Ship-Shape-Amazon-Developer-Hackathon

# Deploy one service:
./deploy/deploy.sh ring-porchpass

# ...or deploy all five at once:
./deploy/deploy-all.sh

Each deploy.sh run builds the service's Docker image, pushes it to a per-service ECR repository, and creates (or updates) an ECS Express Mode service for it, printing the assigned URL when done — typically 3-5 minutes per service, mostly Express Mode's own provisioning time (the ALB, target group, and auto scaling policy it creates).

An optional second argument sets the AWS region (defaults to whatever aws configure get region returns, or us-east-1):

./deploy/deploy.sh firetv-courtside eu-west-1

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Resource Scope Purpose ECR repository (one per service, e.g. hackathon-porchpass) per-service Holds that service's container image ECS Express service (e.g. hackathon-porchpass) in cluster hackathon-express per-service Runs the container behind an ALB with an HTTPS URL ECS cluster hackathon-express shared Holds all five Express services (Express Mode can share one ALB across many services) IAM role ecsTaskExecutionRole shared, AWS's standard name Lets ECS pull images and write logs for task startup IAM role ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices shared, AWS's standard name Lets Express Mode provision/manage the ALB, target groups, and auto scaling Auto scaling target minTaskCount=1, maxTaskCount=1 per-service Pins each service to exactly 1 running task

Why pinned to 1 instance: every service in this repo keeps its demo data (passes, game state, flashcards, routing metrics) in an in-memory store, the same simplification each service's own README documents. Scaling out to multiple tasks would make requests land on inconsistent copies of that in-memory state — fine for a real, database-backed service, not for these demos. Pinning to one task keeps the live demo behaving exactly like running it locally.

Why the two IAM role names matter: ecsTaskExecutionRole and ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices are AWS's own documented default role names, not something invented for this repo — the AWS Console's own "quick create" flow and other ECS tutorials use these exact names too. deploy.sh creates them if they don't already exist and reuses them if they do; teardown-shared.sh deliberately never deletes them automatically, since another ECS workload in your account might depend on a role with one of these names. See that script's output for the manual commands if you're sure it's safe to remove them.

docs.title: Redeploying after a code change
docs.text: Just run deploy.sh again for that service — it detects the existing Express Mode service and pushes the new image to it instead of creating a duplicate.

docs.title: Tearing down
docs.text:
Tear services down as soon as you're done demoing — the Fargate task and Application Load Balancer behind an Express Mode service bill for as long as the service exists, whether or not anything is calling it.

# Tear down one service (its Express Mode service + its ECR repo):
./deploy/teardown.sh ring-porchpass

# Tear down all five, plus the shared cluster (IAM roles are left in place — see below):
./deploy/teardown-all.sh

teardown.sh only removes what's specific to one service — deleting an Express Mode service also cleans up the ALB target group, listener rule, security group, and auto-scaling policy it created (Express Mode owns and manages those itself, unlike a plain aws ecs delete-service). Run ./deploy/teardown-shared.sh once every service has been torn down to remove the now-empty shared cluster (or just use teardown-all.sh, which does both in the right order). The two shared IAM roles are intentionally never auto-deleted — teardown-shared.sh prints the manual commands instead, so you can decide with full knowledge of what else in your account might use them.

docs.title: Files in this directory
docs.text:
deploy/
  lib.sh              Shared config (service name -> Express service name/port map) + small helpers
  deploy.sh            Build, push, and deploy ONE service:        ./deploy/deploy.sh <service-dir> [region]
  teardown.sh          Tear down ONE service:                      ./deploy/teardown.sh <service-dir> [region]
  deploy-all.sh        Deploy all five services in sequence:       ./deploy/deploy-all.sh [region]
  teardown-all.sh      Tear down all five + the shared cluster:    ./deploy/teardown-all.sh [region]
  teardown-shared.sh   Remove the shared cluster (prints IAM-role
                       removal commands rather than running them): ./deploy/teardown-shared.sh [region]

Each deployable service also has its own Dockerfile and .dockerignore (a standard two-stage Node build: npm ci && npm run build in a builder image, then only dist/ + production node_modules in the runtime image) — deploy.sh just builds whichever one lives in the service directory you point it at.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Docker daemon not reachable — in CloudShell this is almost always fixed by opening a fresh CloudShell tab; the Docker daemon can take a moment to become available right after a session starts.
  • Service fails to stabilize / target unhealthy — Express Mode's ALB health check is HTTP-based (not just a TCP check), so the container must actually return 200 on the health-check path. Every service in this repo exposes GET /healthz for exactly this reason, which is what deploy.sh points the check at; check CloudWatch Logs for the service (look under the ECS console's "Logs" tab for the service, or the log group Express Mode created) for the container's stdout/stderr if it's still failing.
  • AccessDenied on iam:CreateRole — the first deploy.sh run for any service needs to create ecsTaskExecutionRole and ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices if they don't already exist. If your IAM identity can't create roles, ask an account admin to create both once (trust policies and policy ARNs are in deploy/lib.sh's ensure_role calls) and rerun deploy.sh — it will detect and reuse the existing roles.
  • Can't find the service URL in the terminal output — deploy.sh does a best-effort scan of the CLI response for anything URL-shaped (see the note at the top of this file on why). If it comes up empty, check the AWS Console: ECS → Clusters → hackathon-express → Services → the service name, or run aws ecs describe-services --cluster hackathon-express --services <service-name> yourself.

docs.title: Devpost Submission Draft — Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon
docs.text: This is a draft of the text to paste into the Devpost submission form(s) at https://amazonappdev2026.devpost.com/. Everything below is drawn from what's actually built and tested in this repo — nothing invented. Two things Devpost requires that can't be produced in this environment are flagged inline: the demo video and, if you choose to record it, live testing against real Amazon hardware/APIs (Ring devices, a Bee wearable, a Fire TV/Vega device, Bedrock credentials).

docs.title: Read this first: how to actually submit (prize eligibility)
docs.text:
Per the hackathon rules (hackathon-ideas/README.md): a project may win at most one track prize + one mini-challenge prize. This repo contains six standalone implementations — one per track (Fire TV, Alexa+, Bee, Ring) plus both mini-challenges (AWS Builder, Open Source) — because you asked for full coverage of every category. For actual submission, that means picking:

  • One track as your primary entry (the strongest, most complete one), and
  • One mini-challenge layered on top, "nearly free to add" per the rules' own advice.

Recommendation: submit HomeOps (Alexa+) as the primary track — it's the deepest implementation (5 rounds: elicitation, sampling, resources/notifications, resumable transport, RBAC, webhooks) and Alexa+ is one of the two $25k top-prize tracks — paired with the Open Source mini-challenge (friction-log-toolkit, a genuinely useful standalone tool, not a throwaway script). The other four implementations (PorchPass, CourtSide, StudyLoop, the model router) are fully working and can each be submitted as separate Devpost projects if you want to be eligible for their tracks too — Devpost allows one account to submit multiple projects to the same hackathon; each one just needs its own project page, since a single project's prize is capped at one track + one mini-challenge.

The sections below are written so each one is a complete, self-contained Devpost project description — copy the one(s) you're submitting.

docs.title: Project 1 — HomeOps (Alexa+ track)
docs.text:
Tagline: A self-hosted MCP server that lets Alexa+ actually run your household — tasks, shopping, budget — instead of handling one command at a time.

Try it out: alexa-homeops-mcp/ · repo: akashtalole/Build-Ship-Shape-Amazon-Developer-Hackathon

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: Alexa+ is built to orchestrate agentic, multi-step requests — but most skills still only handle one isolated command. We wanted to answer "what's due this week, and can you reorder anything running low?" in one turn, which means giving Alexa+ real tools to chain together, not a single intent.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: HomeOps is a self-hosted MCP server (2025-11-25 spec, Streamable HTTP transport) exposing: tasks (list/add/complete/fair auto-assignment), a shopping/low-stock list with elicitation-gated reordering, expense tracking with budget alerts, a natural-language weekly digest generated via MCP sampling (no bundled LLM key — it asks the connected client's own model), calendar sync with streamed progress notifications, and a compound run_morning_briefing tool that chains all of the above into one call. Round 4–5 additions add multi-household Bearer-token auth, role-based access control (full-access vs. read-only tokens), durable file-backed persistence, MCP logging notifications, outbound alert webhooks (HMAC-signed), and recurring task templates.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript + @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, Express for the Streamable HTTP transport, a custom resumable EventStore for reconnect support, file-backed JSON persistence with atomic write-then-rename. Every feature was built test-first against a real MCP client over real HTTP — no mocked protocol calls.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: Getting elicitation right: reorder_item calls the client's own elicitInput() to get real user confirmation before spending, but not every MCP client declares that capability — it had to gracefully fall back to a preview-then-confirm flow instead of erroring. We also hit a genuine protocol bug ourselves: an early outputSchema for run_morning_briefing didn't match the actual Task shape (missing a done: boolean field), caught only because the smoke test used a real schema-validating client instead of asserting on raw text.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: Five rounds of real, tested features (not stubs) — elicitation, sampling, resumable transport, idempotent writes, multi-tenancy, RBAC, and webhooks — all verified via npm test + tsc --noEmit + npm run build before every commit, with zero shortcuts.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: MCP's newer primitives (elicitation, sampling, resource templates with completion, structured output) let a server delegate exactly the parts that need a human or an LLM back to the client, instead of the server needing its own model key or a hand-rolled confirmation flag.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Deploy behind a real Alexa+ Agent Skill registration; swap the file-backed store for DynamoDB for true multi-instance durability; wire real push notifications (SNS) instead of the in-repo notifier stub.

Built with: typescript, node.js, express, model-context-protocol, mcp-sdk, server-sent-events, json, docker, amazon-ecs

docs.title: Project 2 — PorchPass (Ring track)
docs.text:
Tagline: Time-boxed, no-app-required access passes for Ring doorbells — a dog walker or delivery driver taps a link, not a shared code.

Try it out: ring-porchpass/

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: Homeowners need to grant one-off access (a dog walker, a contractor) but sharing a permanent door code or app login is both insecure and awkward. PorchPass issues single-use or time-boxed passes, correlates the visitor's arrival with a real Ring doorbell/motion event, and notifies the homeowner — with zero app or account required on the visitor's side.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Homeowner issues a pass (visitor, validity window, use limit) → visitor taps a magic link, no login → PorchPass correlates the check-in with the nearest Ring doorbell/motion event within a 5-minute window and attaches the snapshot → homeowner is notified → full audit trail. Round 2–4 additions: recurring passes, HMAC-signed webhook ingress from Ring, a live SSE dashboard feed, quiet hours, rate limiting, outbound signed webhooks with retry, bulk/template pass issuance, grace-period extensions, checkout/visit-duration tracking, a traffic analytics report, household member roles, and AES-256-GCM encryption of visitor phone numbers at rest.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript + Express, an interface-isolated RingClient (real integration point) backed by a SimulatedRingClient for full demoability without Ring hardware or partner credentials, HMAC-SHA256 for both inbound webhook verification and outbound delivery signing, an in-memory pub/sub eventBus feeding the SSE stream.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: No Ring hardware or partner API access in this environment — solved by isolating the entire Ring integration behind one interface (src/ringClient.ts) so swapping in the real Ring API is a single-file change, documented explicitly in the README. Also: auditing every response path to make sure a masked phone number is genuinely never exposed once encryption was added — one raw-store read in the test suite confirms no plaintext PII ever touches disk.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: A full, real access-control lifecycle (issue → arrive → correlate → notify → expire/revoke) with ~50 end-to-end HTTP checks, plus production concerns (webhooks, rate limiting, encryption, quiet hours) most hackathon demos skip entirely.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: Designing the Ring integration seam first — before any business logic — made every later round (recurring passes, bulk issuance, analytics) drop in without touching ringClient.ts at all.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Swap SimulatedRingClient for the real Ring Partner API; replace the demo key derivation for PII encryption with AWS KMS envelope encryption (flagged explicitly as a gap in FRICTION_LOG.md).

Built with: typescript, node.js, express, server-sent-events, hmac, webhooks, aes-256-gcm, docker, amazon-ecs

docs.title: Project 3 — CourtSide (Fire TV track)
docs.text:
Tagline: An AI co-commentator that narrates live sports in plain language and answers "why was that a foul?" without leaving the video.

Try it out: firetv-courtside/

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: Casual viewers tune out of unfamiliar or lower-profile games for lack of context — not lack of interest. CourtSide sits alongside a live broadcast, narrating plays and answering spoken or typed questions grounded in the game's actual current state.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Tracks live game state (score/clock/period), ingests play-by-play events and immediately produces plain-language commentary, answers free-form viewer questions grounded in current state and recent plays, and (round 3–4) adds a live SSE commentary push, outbound alert webhooks for watched-team/player events, a personalized-per-viewer watchlist, season-long stats aggregation, auto-generated game recaps, and multi-sport support.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript + Express, a CommentaryProvider interface (the seam a real Bedrock call would sit behind) backed by a deterministic TemplateCommentaryProvider so the whole pipeline is testable headlessly without a Fire TV device or a computer-vision feed.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: This environment can't run a Fire OS/Vega app or a physical Fire TV — so the submission is scoped honestly to the backend commentary service a real overlay app would call, with the exact shape of that integration (GET /games/:id/commentary polling, POST /games/:id/ask for both D-pad and voice input) spelled out in the README rather than glossed over.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: 51/51 automated checks passing across four feature rounds, including a resumable SSE stream and signed outbound webhooks — genuinely production-shaped, not a scripted demo.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: Separating "what's testable headlessly" from "what needs the real device" up front kept the scope honest and let every round ship fully verified instead of half-stubbed.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
A real Vega/Fire OS overlay app; a computer-vision or official play-by-play data feed wired into POST /games/:id/events; swap TemplateCommentaryProvider for a real Bedrock-backed provider.

Built with: typescript, node.js, express, server-sent-events, webhooks, docker, amazon-ecs

docs.title: Project 4 — StudyLoop (Bee track)
docs.text:
Tagline: Turns an ambient study session into spaced-repetition flashcards automatically — no manual note-taking.

Try it out: bee-studyloop/

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: Students lose track of what they actually covered in a study session, and turning ambient conversation into structured review material is friction people skip. StudyLoop automates that conversion end to end.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Ingests a session transcript, generates a summary plus flashcards (Q&A pairing, definition extraction, cloze-deletion fallback), schedules review via a real SM-2 spaced-repetition algorithm, and (round 2–4) adds quiz mode, shared decks, reminders, adaptive difficulty bias, study streaks with permanent badges, a cross-deck daily review-session planner, TSV import/export round-tripping, and on-demand card regeneration.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript + Express, transcript ingestion isolated behind one normalizeTranscript function — documented as the exact seam where Bee's transcript-retrieval MCP tool would plug in, since it already returns the same {speaker, text, timestampMs} shape this repo defines independently.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: No physical Bee device or Apple Watch in this environment. Rather than fake a device integration, we designed the ingestion contract to match Bee's actual documented output shape, so the "todo" for a real integration is a single sync job, not a rewrite.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: 68/68 checks passing across four rounds, including a full spaced-repetition scheduler implemented as pure, independently-testable functions.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: An accurate, real spaced-repetition algorithm (SM-2) is not meaningfully harder to implement correctly than a fake one — so there was no reason to stub it.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Wire a real Bee MCP get_transcript call into normalizeTranscript's existing array branch; swap TemplateFlashcardGenerator for an LLM-backed generator behind the same interface.

Built with: typescript, node.js, express, sm-2-algorithm, docker, amazon-ecs

docs.title: Project 5 — Model Router (AWS Builder mini-challenge)
docs.text:
Tagline: A SageMaker-sidecar-in-front-of-Bedrock routing pattern: cheap and fast for the common case, escalate to a full foundation model only when confidence is low.

Try it out: aws-builder-model-router/

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: Off-the-shelf foundation models are often overkill in cost and latency for narrow, well-defined classification tasks. This is a reusable pattern, demoed via urgency triage for household-automation-style messages (urgent / routine / informational).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Runs a deterministic, explainable sidecar classifier first; if its confidence clears a threshold (default 0.7), returns immediately at sidecar cost/latency; otherwise escalates to a foundation-model-shaped provider. Rounds 2–4 add response caching, a circuit breaker with fallback, shadow evaluation, an adaptive confidence threshold, streaming responses, rate limiting, a three-tier cascade, cost budgets (global and per-caller), canary/A-B sidecar routing, outbound alert webhooks, and Prometheus-format metrics export.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript + Express, both the sidecar and the foundation model behind interfaces shaped exactly like the real SageMaker/Bedrock SDKs, backed by mock providers — documented so the swap to real AWS services touches only two files.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: No AWS credentials available in this environment, so proving the pattern (not the API call) is correct meant building an honest cost/latency model for each path and verifying routing decisions and budget/circuit-breaker behavior deterministically in tests, rather than trusting a live call.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: 78/78 checks passing through four rounds of genuinely production-shaped concerns — canary rollout, per-caller budgets, Prometheus export — on top of the core routing pattern.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: A routing decision's correctness (confidence-based escalation, budget enforcement, circuit-breaker tripping) is fully testable without ever calling a real model, as long as the provider interface is honest about what a real call would cost and how long it would take.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Swap MockSidecarClassifier/MockBedrockProvider for real SageMaker endpoint + Bedrock InvokeModel calls behind the same interfaces; persist metrics to CloudWatch instead of the local JSON file.

Built with: typescript, node.js, express, aws, sagemaker, bedrock, prometheus, docker, amazon-ecs

docs.title: Project 6 — friction-log-toolkit (Open Source mini-challenge)
docs.text:
Tagline: A CLI that makes capturing a hackathon friction log as cheap as one terminal command, in the moment it happens — not reconstructed from memory an hour before the deadline.

Try it out: friction-log-toolkit/

docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: This hackathon's own rules reward a well-written friction log with up to a 10% judging bonus — but in practice, friction logs get written from memory right before submission, after the specific error messages and dead-end docs pages are already forgotten. This tool exists to fix that process gap for every team, not just this one.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: friction-log init / add "..." --tag friction / list / export turns captured points into a structured Markdown report in the exact "what worked / friction / feature requests" shape used by every other project in this repo. Rounds 2–4 add stats, config, git-aware auto-tagging, multi-format export, entry merge/edit/remove, full-text search, a local dashboard server, a watch mode REPL, push/pull sync between two instances, reusable entry templates, an ASCII stats chart, and keyword-based auto-tag suggestions.

docs.title: How we built it
docs.text: TypeScript CLI (node:http for the dashboard — no framework dependency), a portable TSV/JSON export format for interop with the Bee track's flashcard import.

docs.title: Challenges we ran into
docs.text: A genuine bug surfaced while testing sync: driving the test via a blocking execFileSync against a fake remote server hosted in the same test process deadlocks, since the blocking call freezes the event loop the remote handler itself needs — fixed with a spawn-based async test helper, and documented in FRICTION_LOG.md as a real lesson for anyone testing loopback HTTP calls this way.

docs.title: Accomplishments we're proud of
docs.text: 137/137 checks across four rounds, plus genuine dogfooding — this tool's own FRICTION_LOG.md entries were captured with itself while building it.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text: The most valuable open-source contribution here isn't a huge feature — it's removing the specific five seconds of friction (context-switching to write something down) that causes documentation to never get written at all.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Publish to npm; add a GitHub Action that opens a PR comment summarizing captured friction points automatically at PR time.

Built with: typescript, node.js, cli, git

docs.title: Cross-cutting notes for every project (paste into "Product feedback" fields)
docs.text:
• Tools used: Node.js/TypeScript throughout; @modelcontextprotocol/sdk for HomeOps; Express for every HTTP service; no external LLM/cloud calls anywhere (all AI- and AWS-shaped seams are interfaces backed by deterministic mocks, documented per-project as the exact swap-in point).
  • What worked well: isolating every hardware/cloud dependency (Ring, Bee, Fire TV, Bedrock, SageMaker) behind a single interface let every feature round ship fully tested without ever needing real credentials or hardware.
  • What didn't / platform friction: AWS App Runner closed to new customers on 2026-04-30 mid-way through building the deploy tooling — the CloudShell deploy scripts in deploy/ were rewritten to target Amazon ECS Express Mode instead once this was confirmed, and that migration itself is documented as a friction-log-worthy platform change.
  • Onboarding: every project's own README.md has copy-pasteable curl examples and a npm install && npm test && npm run build verification sequence; deploy/README.md covers taking any of the five backend services live from AWS CloudShell with zero local setup.
  • Full friction logs: see each project's own FRICTION_LOG.md for the complete, dated list of friction points, feature requests, and design trade-offs encountered while building it.

Decide whether to merge more of them in before the Oct 23, 2026 deadline, and link the exact commit/branch you're submitting if you leave any unmerged.

docs.title: Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon — Winning Idea Playbook
docs.text:
Source material: Rules · Overview · Resources

This folder distills the hackathon's judging criteria into a set of top candidate winning ideas per prize category. Each file covers one track/mini-challenge and proposes 3 concepts, scored against the four equally-weighted judging criteria:

  1. Tech Implementation — effective use of required APIs/SDKs/device capabilities
  2. Design — a complete, coherent, intuitive product experience for the target device
  3. Potential Impact — solves a genuine customer need, viable beyond the hackathon
  4. Quality of Idea — creative, ecosystem-aware use of the required tools

A friction log (documenting pain points while building) earns up to a 10% judging bonus in every track — every idea below recommends keeping one.

docs.title: Alexa+ Track — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prizes: $25,000 + $15K AWS credits + Amazon meeting (1st) · $15,000 + $5K AWS credits (2nd) · $4,000 + $1K AWS credits (3rd) Required tech: An Agent Skill or a self-hosted MCP server (spec 2025-11-25 or later), using open standards for Agent Skills and Streamable HTTP transport; simulate via the provided web app Guidance: Build MCP integrations using open standards; prioritize genuinely useful, agentic tasks Alexa+ can hand off to

docs.title: Idea 1: "HomeOps" — Household Operations MCP Skill (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: Running a household means juggling many small services (grocery reorder, bill tracking, appointment scheduling, chore rotation) that Alexa+ can't currently reason across.

Solution: A self-hosted MCP server exposing tools for a unified household "ops" system — Alexa+ can be asked "what's due this week" or "reorder anything running low" and the agent orchestrates across connected tools (calendar, shopping list, simple budget tracker).

  • Tech Implementation: MCP server (Streamable HTTP transport, 2025-11-25+ spec) exposing well-scoped tools (list_upcoming_tasks, reorder_item, add_expense) with clear input/output schemas so Alexa+'s agent can chain them.
  • Design: Conversational flows feel like delegating to a competent assistant, not issuing single commands; confirms before any purchase/spend action.
  • Potential Impact: Broad household applicability; a real reason to keep an MCP server running daily, not just for the demo.
  • Quality of Idea: Demonstrates multi-tool agentic orchestration, which is exactly what distinguishes an "Agent Skill" from a legacy Alexa Skill.

docs.title: Idea 2: "DevDesk" — Developer Productivity Agent Skill
docs.text:
Problem: Developers want hands-free status checks (build status, PR review queue, incident alerts) without switching context away from what they're doing.

Solution: An MCP server that lets Alexa+ answer "what's blocking me today" by querying GitHub/CI/ticket systems, and can take safe actions (approve a routine PR, snooze a non-urgent alert) via voice.

  • Tech Implementation: MCP tools wrapping GitHub/CI APIs; read-only tools by default, explicit confirmation for any state-changing tool call.
  • Design: Short, information-dense voice responses; a companion web view via the Alexa+ web app to show detail (PR diffs, alert lists) when useful.
  • Potential Impact: Speaks directly to the "AWS Builder" developer audience — plausible daily-use tool for engineering teams, not just a hackathon demo.
  • Quality of Idea: Shows a non-obvious, work-context use of Alexa+ beyond home/media use cases — differentiates from the flood of home-automation submissions.

docs.title: Idea 3: "CareCheck" — Caregiver Coordination Skill
docs.text:
Problem: Families coordinating care for an aging or ill relative rely on scattered texts/calls to track medication, visits, and needs.

Solution: An MCP-backed Alexa+ skill that lets a caregiver ask "has mom taken her afternoon meds" or "who's visiting this week," pulling from a shared care log that any family member (or the Ring/Bee ecosystem) can also feed.

  • Tech Implementation: MCP server backed by a simple shared datastore; tools for logging and querying care events; can cross-reference with a Ring doorbell event log for "who visited today" if paired with the Ring track.
  • Design: Reassuring, low-friction voice interactions for often-stressed caregivers; clear, calm confirmations.
  • Potential Impact: Strong social-good angle with a real recurring need; extensible ecosystem story ties Alexa+ + Ring + Bee together, which the hackathon explicitly encourages ("connect the living room, the front door, and the cloud").
  • Quality of Idea: Cross-track integration story is a distinctive way to demonstrate ecosystem understanding.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: Each idea centers on genuine multi-step delegation (the core differentiator of Agent Skills/MCP vs. classic voice commands), uses the required Streamable HTTP MCP transport, and can be demoed live against the Alexa+ web app simulator. Idea 3 also offers a natural bridge to the Ring track for teams wanting a cross-ecosystem submission — but remember only one track prize can be won per project, so use that bridge for demo richness, not for double-prize strategy.

docs.title: AWS Builder Mini-Challenge — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prize: $5,000 + $5K AWS credits + Amazon meeting (1 winner) Required tech: Meaningfully incorporate AWS services such as Bedrock, AgentCore, SageMaker, Strands SDK, or Kiro Note: Can be stacked with any one primary track submission (Fire TV, Alexa+, Bee, or Ring) — max one track prize + one mini-challenge prize per project

docs.title: Idea 1: "Bring your own brain" — Bedrock/AgentCore backend for any primary-track idea (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: Most compelling hackathon ideas need an AI reasoning layer, but teams often bolt on a generic LLM call as an afterthought rather than a genuine AWS-native agent architecture.

Solution: Rather than treating AWS Builder as a separate project, design the primary track's AI features (e.g., Fire TV's "CourtSide" commentary, Alexa+'s "HomeOps" orchestration, or Ring's "StoreWatch" analytics) around Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for multi-step agent orchestration and Strands SDK for tool-calling, with SageMaker for any custom model (e.g., computer-vision tagging).

  • Tech Implementation: AgentCore session/runtime for agent state; Strands SDK to define and register tools cleanly; Bedrock foundation models for generation/reasoning; SageMaker endpoint for any bespoke model.
  • Design: Invisible to the end user — the win is architectural rigor (retries, observability, tool schemas) rather than a new UI.
  • Potential Impact: A well-built agent backend is directly reusable infrastructure, independent of which device track it powers.
  • Quality of Idea: Judges for this mini-challenge are specifically evaluating AWS-service depth, not novelty of the end-user idea, so this is the lowest-risk, highest-synergy way to add the mini-challenge without a second parallel project.

docs.title: Idea 2: "Kiro Crew" — Multi-Agent Content Pipeline
docs.text:
Problem: Building the kind of AI-enhanced content pipelines the tracks reward (e.g., Fire TV's scene-tagging, Bee's summarization) usually means hand-writing orchestration glue code.

Solution: Use Kiro (spec-driven, agentic development) to define and generate a multi-agent pipeline — e.g., a "tagging agent," a "summarization agent," and a "QA agent" — that processes content for whichever primary track needs it, with the Kiro spec and generated code included as part of the submission.

  • Tech Implementation: Kiro specs driving codegen for each pipeline agent; Strands SDK or AgentCore for agent-to-agent handoff; Bedrock models doing the actual generation work.
  • Design: Submission includes the Kiro spec files themselves as part of the "quality of idea" story — showing spec-driven, reviewable AI development rather than ad hoc prompting.
  • Potential Impact: Demonstrates a repeatable engineering pattern other developers could adopt, not just a one-off feature.
  • Quality of Idea: Directly showcases the newest tool in the required list (Kiro), which stands out among submissions that default to a plain Bedrock API call.

docs.title: Idea 3: "SageMaker Sidecar" — Custom On-Device-Adjacent ML Model
docs.text:
Problem: Off-the-shelf foundation models are often overkill (cost/latency) for narrow, well-defined tasks like the computer-vision scoring in Fire TV's "FamilyPlay" or Ring's traffic analytics.

Solution: Train and deploy a small, purpose-built model on SageMaker (e.g., a lightweight motion-classification or traffic-counting model) as a fast, cheap "sidecar" that the primary track's app calls before falling back to a larger Bedrock model for anything ambiguous.

  • Tech Implementation: SageMaker training job + real-time or serverless inference endpoint; primary app calls the SageMaker endpoint first, escalating to Bedrock only when confidence is low.
  • Design: End users never see this layer directly, but its effect is faster, cheaper, more responsive core features.
  • Potential Impact: Shows engineering maturity — using the right-sized model for the job is a real production consideration judges will recognize.
  • Quality of Idea: Differentiates from submissions that only call Bedrock, since it demonstrates SageMaker specifically.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: The AWS Builder mini-challenge is judged on genuine, well-architected AWS usage rather than a standalone idea — so the strongest strategy is to fold one of these patterns directly into whichever primary track submission a team is already building, maximizing shared demo time and effort while still meeting the "meaningfully incorporate AWS services" bar.

docs.title: Bee Track — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prizes: $12,000 + Amazon meeting (1st) · $8,000 (2nd) Required tech: Data from an actual Bee wearable device, or an Apple Watch running Bee software Guidance: Integrate Bee's CLI, MCP server, or Agent Skills; prioritize education, developer experience, and productivity applications

docs.title: Idea 1: "StudyLoop" — Ambient Study Session Coach (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: Students lose track of what they actually discussed/decided in study sessions and struggle to convert ambient conversation into structured review material.

Solution: A tool that uses Bee's always-on ambient capture to auto-generate spaced-repetition flashcards and session summaries from study group conversations or lectures, surfaced through a simple daily review app.

  • Tech Implementation: Bee MCP server/CLI pulls transcribed conversation segments; an LLM pipeline extracts key facts/questions and formats them as flashcards; a lightweight companion app schedules spaced-repetition review.
  • Design: Zero manual note-taking required; a clean daily "review your day" flow that respects that ambient audio is sensitive (clear opt-in/recording indicators, easy delete).
  • Potential Impact: Directly hits "education," one of the explicitly prioritized categories, with an everyday, recurring use case for students.
  • Quality of Idea: Turns passive ambient capture into an active learning loop — a genuinely novel use of wearable AI rather than a simple transcript viewer.

docs.title: Idea 2: "DevContext" — Ambient Developer Journal & Standup Generator
docs.text:
Problem: Developers forget what they worked on and why by the time standup or a retro comes around, and manually logging decisions is friction they skip.

Solution: A Bee-powered tool that captures ambient work conversations (pairing sessions, debugging mutters, meetings) and turns them into a searchable daily dev journal plus an auto-drafted standup update.

  • Tech Implementation: Bee MCP server feeding a pipeline that tags entries by topic/project, then generates a daily summary; CLI integration lets developers query past context ("what did we decide about the caching bug last Tuesday?").
  • Design: Minimal-friction, ambient-first — the value is that the developer does nothing extra; summaries are terse and skimmable.
  • Potential Impact: Hits both "developer experience" and "productivity," the two other prioritized categories; plausible tie-in with the AWS Builder mini-challenge if the summarization pipeline runs on Bedrock.
  • Quality of Idea: Demonstrates a clear before/after productivity win that's easy to show in a 3-minute demo.

docs.title: Idea 3: "LangPractice" — Real-World Language Immersion Coach
docs.text:
Problem: Language learners get plenty of app-based drilling but little feedback on their real, spontaneous conversations.

Solution: A Bee-based coach that (with consent) reviews real conversational speech throughout the day, flags recurring grammar/vocabulary mistakes, and generates a personalized practice set each evening.

  • Tech Implementation: Bee ambient transcript pull via MCP; a language-analysis LLM pass identifies error patterns; nightly digest with 5–10 targeted exercises.
  • Design: Strong emphasis on privacy affordances (per-language opt-in, easy pause); friendly, non-judgmental coaching tone.
  • Potential Impact: Clear education-category fit with a distinctive "real life is the textbook" angle.
  • Quality of Idea: Creative reuse of ambient capture for a use case beyond note-taking/productivity, showing ecosystem understanding.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: All three lean into what makes Bee unique — ambient, always-on capture — rather than treating it as just another dictation tool, and each maps cleanly to one of the three explicitly prioritized categories (education, developer experience, productivity). Idea 1 or 2 is the safer bet for judged "Potential Impact," since both address large, recurring audiences (students, developers).

docs.title: Fire TV Track — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prizes: $25,000 + $15K AWS credits + Amazon meeting (1st) · $15,000 + $5K AWS credits (2nd) · $4,000 + $1K AWS credits (3rd) Required tech: Deployable on Fire OS or Vega OS; any framework accepted (React Native, web, native Android/Kotlin/Java) Prioritized categories: AI-enhanced viewing, sports, fitness, family entertainment, multi-modal UX, computer vision Starter kits: React Native multi-TV app sample, Vega video/sports/audio samples, TV interface patterns, native Kotlin/Jetpack Compose

docs.title: Idea 1: "CourtSide" — AI Co-Commentator for Live Sports (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: Casual sports viewers tune out during unfamiliar or lower-profile games because they lack context (rules, player stats, stakes).

Solution: A Fire TV app that overlays a real-time, voice- and text-based AI companion on any live sports stream — explaining plays, surfacing stats, and answering spoken questions ("why was that a foul?") without leaving the video.

  • Tech Implementation: Vega/Fire OS video app with a picture-in-picture or overlay panel; computer vision on the game feed (or paired play-by-play API) drives a Bedrock-based LLM commentary layer; remote/voice input for on-demand Q&A.
  • Design: 10-foot UI overlay that never blocks the score bug or key action; D-pad and voice both drive the same experience; auto-hides during high-action moments.
  • Potential Impact: Big-tent appeal (new fans, second-screen replacement, accessibility for viewers unfamiliar with a sport); clear app-store path as a companion layer across leagues.
  • Quality of Idea: Combines multi-modal UX + AI-enhanced viewing + sports, three prioritized categories at once.
  • Mini-challenge stack: Pairs naturally with AWS Builder (Bedrock for commentary generation, SageMaker/computer vision for play detection).

docs.title: Idea 2: "FamilyPlay" — Multi-Modal Family Fitness & Trivia Hub
docs.text:
Problem: Family entertainment apps on TV are passive; there's no lightweight, camera-optional way to turn the living room into a shared activity space.

Solution: A Fire TV app combining short fitness challenges, cooperative trivia, and karaoke-style games, using the remote, phone-as-controller, and optional camera-based motion scoring, with adaptive difficulty per family member.

  • Tech Implementation: Fire OS app using Fire TV's input APIs (remote, voice, second-screen companion), optional on-device computer vision for movement scoring.
  • Design: Big, legible 10-foot UI; simple onboarding for kids and grandparents alike; session summaries at the end of each round.
  • Potential Impact: Recurring, everyday use case; monetizable as a subscription family-activity app.
  • Quality of Idea: Directly hits family entertainment + fitness + multi-modal UX.

docs.title: Idea 3: "SceneSense" — Computer-Vision Content Discovery
docs.text:
Problem: Viewers often want "more like this scene" (mood, actor, setting) but search is limited to title/genre metadata.

Solution: A Fire TV discovery app that uses computer vision on trailers/thumbnails plus an AI recommendation layer to let users search visually ("shows with cozy cabin vibes," "movies with this actor's other roles") and get personalized rows.

  • Tech Implementation: Batch computer-vision tagging pipeline (can run on AWS) + Bedrock for natural-language query understanding; Fire TV front-end renders standard TV row/carousel UI.
  • Design: Familiar Fire TV discovery UX (rows, carousels) so it feels native, with a voice-first search entry point.
  • Potential Impact: Solves real content-discovery pain across any content library; extensible to any catalog.
  • Quality of Idea: Strong computer-vision + AI-enhanced viewing combination.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: All three map to at least two of the six prioritized Fire TV categories, use required device input modalities (remote/voice/companion), and are demoable in under 3 minutes on real Fire OS/Vega hardware or emulator. Recommend building idea 1 or 2 as the primary submission and stacking the AWS Builder mini-challenge on top (near-zero extra scope since AI backends already use AWS services).

docs.title: Open Source Mini-Challenge — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prize: $5,000 + $5K AWS credits + Amazon meeting (1 winner) Required tech: A new public repository, or a meaningful contribution (PR, branch, or fork) to an existing public repository Note: Can be stacked with any one primary track submission — max one track prize + one mini-challenge prize per project

docs.title: Idea 1: "Amazon Devices Starter Kits+" — Contribute back to Amazon's own sample repos (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: The official starter samples (React Native multi-TV app, Vega video/sports/audio samples, ring-api-helloworld) are useful but inevitably leave gaps teams discover while building their primary track submission.

Solution: While building a primary track project, generalize a genuinely reusable piece (a hook, a UI component, a helper module, a bug fix) and submit it as a pull request back to the relevant Amazon amazonappdev sample repository, with tests and documentation.

  • Tech Implementation: Real PR with a clear description, tests, and adherence to the target repo's contribution guidelines.
  • Design: N/A (developer-facing), but code quality, docs, and PR description quality all matter for judging.
  • Potential Impact: Directly benefits every future hackathon participant and Amazon Devices developer — about as legible an "impact beyond the hackathon" story as this category allows.
  • Quality of Idea: Judges can literally see the contribution accepted/reviewed upstream, which is strong, hard-to-fake evidence of quality.

docs.title: Idea 2: "MCP Toolkit for Amazon Devices" — New open-source library
docs.text:
Problem: Teams across Fire TV, Alexa+, Bee, and Ring all end up writing similar MCP server boilerplate (auth, schema validation, Streamable HTTP transport setup) from scratch.

Solution: Publish a new, focused open-source npm/PyPI package — e.g., a minimal MCP server scaffold with Streamable HTTP transport, schema helpers, and example tools — that any team (including ones outside this hackathon) can build on for Alexa+ Agent Skills or Bee integrations.

  • Tech Implementation: New public repo with clean package structure, README, examples, and a permissive license (MIT/Apache-2.0); ideally used by the team's own primary-track submission as a dogfooding proof point.
  • Design: Clear README with a "quickstart in 5 minutes" example.
  • Potential Impact: Lowers the barrier for the entire Amazon Agent Skill/MCP developer ecosystem, not just this hackathon.
  • Quality of Idea: A genuinely reusable library (not a hackathon-only demo repo) stands out; strengthen it with CI, tests, and a couple of external stars/usage if time allows.

docs.title: Idea 3: "Friction Log Toolkit" — Tooling that turns friction logs into structured feedback
docs.text:
Problem: The hackathon explicitly rewards friction logs (up to 10% bonus) but there's no standard tooling for capturing them systematically.

Solution: Build and open-source a small CLI/template tool that helps developers capture friction points (timestamped notes, tagged by API/SDK, exportable as a structured Markdown report) while building for any Amazon Devices track — then use it to produce the team's own friction log submission.

  • Tech Implementation: New public repo — a simple CLI (friction log start, friction log add "note", friction log export) with Markdown output matching common hackathon feedback formats.
  • Design: Near-zero friction to use (irony intended) — a single command to log an issue in the moment.
  • Potential Impact: Directly useful to every other hackathon participant and to Amazon's own developer-experience team as structured feedback.
  • Quality of Idea: Meta and self-referential in a way that's memorable to judges, while still being a genuinely useful, novel tool.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: Idea 1 is the safest and highest-impact choice because contributions to Amazon's own repos are directly visible to the judges and the Amazon Developer team who reviews them. Ideas 2 and 3 are stronger if a team wants full ownership of a new project, and both naturally produce artifacts (a library, a friction-log export) that also strengthen the primary track submission's "Product Feedback" and friction-log bonus sections.

docs.title: Ring Track — Top Winning Ideas
docs.text: Prizes: $12,000 + Amazon meeting (1st) · $8,000 (2nd) Required tech: Ring APIs, SDKs, simulators, or devices per Ring developer docs Prioritized categories: access control, business systems, IoT automation, accessibility, care-taking Starter sample: ring-api-helloworld

docs.title: Idea 1: "PorchPass" — Delegated, Time-Boxed Access Control (Recommended top pick)
docs.text:
Problem: Homeowners frequently need to grant one-time or short-window access (dog walker, delivery, contractor, guest) but sharing a permanent code or app login is insecure and inconvenient.

Solution: A Ring-integrated app that lets a homeowner issue single-use or time-boxed "passes" tied to a visitor's phone number; Ring's doorbell/camera events confirm arrival and automatically notify the homeowner with a short clip when the pass is used, then auto-expire it.

  • Tech Implementation: Ring API integration for event webhooks (doorbell press, motion) and camera snapshot/clip retrieval; simple pass-issuing backend with expiring tokens; SMS/notification hook for the visitor.
  • Design: A two-tap "grant access" flow for the homeowner and a no-app-required flow for the visitor (SMS link); clear audit trail of who came and when.
  • Potential Impact: Squarely hits "access control" with a real, everyday pain point (dog walkers, short-term rentals, small businesses).
  • Quality of Idea: Goes beyond simple notification apps by adding a lightweight access-delegation layer on top of Ring's event stream.

docs.title: Idea 2: "StoreWatch" — Small-Business Ring Operations Dashboard
docs.text:
Problem: Small storefronts (shops, salons, home-based businesses) use Ring cameras for security but get no operational insight — foot traffic patterns, peak hours, or unattended-entry alerts.

Solution: A business-systems dashboard that aggregates Ring camera/doorbell events into traffic analytics, staffing recommendations, and instant alerts for after-hours entry, tailored for non-technical small-business owners.

  • Tech Implementation: Ring API for event history and live snapshots; lightweight analytics backend (could run on AWS for the mini-challenge) aggregating visit counts/time-of-day; simple web dashboard.
  • Design: Plain-language insights ("Tuesdays 2–4pm are your busiest window") rather than raw event logs; mobile-friendly for owners on the go.
  • Potential Impact: Direct fit for "business systems," with a believable path to real small-business adoption.
  • Quality of Idea: Repurposes security hardware as a business-intelligence tool — a genuinely different angle than most home-security demos.

docs.title: Idea 3: "SafeCheck" — Accessible Care-Taking Companion
docs.text:
Problem: Family members caring for an elderly or disabled relative living independently want reassurance without invasive monitoring, and need alerts that respect the person's autonomy.

Solution: A Ring-based check-in system that uses doorbell/entry events plus a simple "I'm OK" voice or button confirmation flow, escalating to a caregiver only if expected daily activity (e.g., getting the mail, a morning door open) doesn't occur — with an accessible, high-contrast/voice-first interface for the person being cared for.

  • Tech Implementation: Ring API for entry/motion event patterns; a rules engine for expected-activity windows; escalation notifications to designated caregivers; accessible companion UI (large text, voice prompts).
  • Design: Explicitly designed for accessibility (screen-reader friendly, minimal required interaction) and for dignity — reassurance, not surveillance.
  • Potential Impact: Directly combines two prioritized categories — accessibility and care-taking — into one coherent product with a compelling social-good story.
  • Quality of Idea: Thoughtful handling of consent/privacy for a vulnerable user group demonstrates strong design maturity, a key judging criterion.

docs.title: Why these win
docs.text: Each idea targets two of the five prioritized Ring categories at once (access control, business systems, IoT automation, accessibility, care-taking), uses real Ring event/API data rather than mocked footage, and tells a clear "who is this for and why do they need it" story for the Potential Impact criterion. Idea 3 pairs especially well with the Alexa+ "CareCheck" concept if a team wants a cross-ecosystem demo (see alexa-plus.md).

docs.title: CourtSide (Fire TV)
