docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
npm install
npm run build
npm start
# PorchPass listening on http://localhost:4444

Or for local iteration: npm run dev

docs.title: Environment variables (all optional)
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose PORT 4444 HTTP port RING_WEBHOOK_SECRET a clearly-marked local-dev-only default HMAC secret for POST /ring/events (see §3) QUIET_HOURS_START / QUIET_HOURS_END unset (no quiet hours) Initial quiet-hours window ("HH:MM", UTC) — can also be set at runtime via POST /settings PORCHPASS_ENCRYPTION_KEY a clearly-marked local-dev-only default Key material for AES-256-GCM encryption of visitor PII at rest (see §4 of Round 4 additions)

docs.title: Try it by hand
docs.text:
# 1. Issue a pass valid for the next 2 hours
curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker",
  "visitorPhone": "+15551234567",
  "validUntil": "2026-09-02T18:00:00Z",
  "note": "dog walker"
}'
# -> note the checkinToken in the response, and watch the console for the "SMS" the visitor received

# 2. Simulate a doorbell press (stands in for Ring's real webhook — now signed, see "Webhook signature
#    verification" below for why)
BODY='{"deviceId": "front-door", "type": "ding"}'
SIGNATURE=$(node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').createHmac('sha256', process.argv[1]).update(process.argv[2]).digest('hex'))" \
  "porchpass-local-dev-secret-DO-NOT-USE-IN-PRODUCTION" "$BODY")
curl -X POST localhost:4444/ring/events -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Ring-Signature: $SIGNATURE" -d "$BODY"

# 3. Visit the check-in link in a browser, or simulate the visitor's tap:
curl -X POST localhost:4444/checkin/<checkinToken> -H "Accept: application/json"

# 4. See the audit trail
curl localhost:4444/visits

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
npm test

Starts the server on an ephemeral port and drives the full lifecycle over real HTTP requests: issuing a pass sends a (simulated) SMS with a check-in link; a simulated doorbell event plus a visitor check-in produces a correlated visit with a snapshot URL and a homeowner notification; a single-use pass rejects a second check-in; a maxUses: 2 pass allows exactly two; a revoked pass and an expired pass both correctly deny access — then a second round covers every feature in Advanced features, a third round covers every feature in Round 3 additions, and a fourth round covers every feature in Round 4 additions below — including spinning up a real local HTTP listener in the test process to receive and verify an outbound webhook delivery, and reaching directly into the in-memory store (store.ts) to confirm a visitor's phone number is never present in plaintext anywhere in the raw stored record, not just absent from the API's response shape. No external services required.

docs.title: Advanced features
docs.text: Six additions on top of the v1 lifecycle, aimed at the kind of depth a real access-control service needs in production, not just a demo.

docs.title: 1. Idempotency-key protected issuance
docs.text:
POST /passes accepts an optional idempotencyKey. Retrying the exact same issuance request (e.g. a mobile client that isn't sure whether its first request made it through a flaky connection) with the same key returns the original pass — no duplicate pass, no duplicate "you have access" SMS to the visitor. This mirrors how any real payment or side-effecting API protects a retried request (Stripe, for example, does the same thing). Implemented as a small idempotencyKey -> passId cache in store.ts, checked before a new pass is ever created.

curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker", "visitorPhone": "+15551234567",
  "validUntil": "2026-09-02T18:00:00Z", "idempotencyKey": "dog-walker-tuesday-001"
}'
# Run the exact same request again — same pass ID comes back, no second SMS sent.
curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker", "visitorPhone": "+15551234567",
  "validUntil": "2026-09-02T18:00:00Z", "idempotencyKey": "dog-walker-tuesday-001"
}'

docs.title: 2. Recurring passes
docs.text:
Instead of only a fixed one-off validFrom/validUntil window, a pass can carry a recurrence rule:

{ "daysOfWeek": [2, 4], "startTime": "13:00", "endTime": "15:00" }

daysOfWeek uses 0=Sunday..6=Saturday; startTime/endTime are "HH:MM" 24-hour clock values, interpreted in UTC for consistency in this demo (a real deployment would store the household's IANA timezone alongside the rule). validFrom/validUntil still apply as the outer bounds of the whole schedule (e.g. "good for the next 90 days") — the recurrence rule narrows validity further, to only the matching day-of-week/time-of-day slices within that range. This is the realistic fix for "the weekly dog walker doesn't need a brand-new pass issued every week." One-off passes that omit recurrence behave exactly as before — this is additive, not a breaking change. recurrence.ts also handles a window that crosses midnight (startTime > endTime, e.g. an overnight "22:00" -> "02:00" sitter window).

curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker", "visitorPhone": "+15551234567",
  "validUntil": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z",
  "recurrence": { "daysOfWeek": [2, 4], "startTime": "13:00", "endTime": "15:00" },
  "note": "dog walker, Tue/Thu afternoons"
}'

docs.title: 3. Webhook signature verification
docs.text:
POST /ring/events — the Ring event ingress — now verifies an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw request body against a shared secret, rejecting missing or invalid signatures with 401. This mirrors how Ring's real webhook delivery authenticates callers, and closes off the obvious hole in leaving a public event-ingress endpoint unauthenticated: without it, anyone who finds the URL could forge doorbell/motion events. The secret comes from RING_WEBHOOK_SECRET; if unset, a clearly-marked local-dev-only default (DEFAULT_DEV_WEBHOOK_SECRET in webhookAuth.ts) is used so the demo and tests work with zero configuration — never rely on that default outside local development. webhookAuth.ts exports signPayload(secret, rawBody), the same helper the test suite and any real Ring integration would use to compute the X-Ring-Signature header.

SECRET="porchpass-local-dev-secret-DO-NOT-USE-IN-PRODUCTION"  # or your $RING_WEBHOOK_SECRET
BODY='{"deviceId":"front-door","type":"ding"}'
SIGNATURE=$(node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').createHmac('sha256', process.argv[1]).update(process.argv[2]).digest('hex'))" "$SECRET" "$BODY")

curl -X POST localhost:4444/ring/events \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Ring-Signature: $SIGNATURE" \
  -d "$BODY"
# A request with no X-Ring-Signature header (or a wrong one) gets 401.

docs.title: 4. Real-time homeowner event stream
docs.text:
GET /events/stream opens a Server-Sent Events connection: a homeowner's dashboard can hold it open and receive a pushed pass_issued, visit_checkin, pass_revoked, or pass_expired event the instant it happens, instead of polling GET /visits. GET /visits is unchanged and still the audit-trail source of truth — the stream is a purely additive real-time layer on top, backed by a small pub/sub (eventBus.ts) that passService.ts publishes to on every state-changing action.

curl -N localhost:4444/events/stream
# In another terminal, issue a pass or check a visitor in — the first terminal
# immediately prints an `event: pass_issued` / `event: visit_checkin` frame.

docs.title: 5. Quiet-hours enforcement
docs.text:
POST /settings sets a household-level quiet-hours window ({ "quietHours": { "start": "22:00", "end": "07:00" } }, UTC, and handles crossing midnight the same way recurrence.ts does). Once set, POST /checkin/:token rejects check-ins during that window with a clear reason — even for a pass whose own validFrom/validUntil or recurrence window would otherwise allow it — unless the pass explicitly opts out with "allowQuietHours": true (e.g. a pass for an overnight nurse or a legitimately late delivery). This layers a security-conscious household policy on top of, not instead of, ordinary pass validity.

curl -X POST localhost:4444/settings -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"quietHours": {"start": "22:00", "end": "07:00"}}'
curl localhost:4444/settings   # see the current setting
# Clear it again:
curl -X POST localhost:4444/settings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"quietHours": null}'

docs.title: 6. Rate limiting on check-in attempts
docs.text: POST /checkin/:token is, by design, the one endpoint in the system that doesn't require an account or login — that's the whole point of the no-app-required flow, but it also makes it the one place someone could try to brute-force or guess a checkinToken. Each token is capped at 5 check-in attempts per rolling 10-minute window (valid or invalid tokens both count, since an unknown token is exactly what a guesser sends); the 6th attempt within the window gets 429 with a clear "too many attempts" message. Implemented as an in-memory sliding window in rateLimiter.ts — see FRICTION_LOG.md for the multi-instance-deployment caveat that comes with that choice.

docs.title: Round 3 additions
docs.text: Four more additions on top of everything above: multi-device support, outbound webhook notifications, bulk/template pass issuance, and a grace-period extension flow for a visitor who just missed their window.

docs.title: 1. Multi-device support
docs.text:
Every device reference used to be hardcoded to a single "front-door" id. Now PorchPass has a small device registry (devices.ts): a Device is { id, name, registeredAt, registeredVia }, and a device needs no separate setup step to be usable — the first pass that names it in deviceIds, or the first Ring event that arrives for it, registers it right then with a name derived from the id ("back-door" → "Back Door"). POST /devices is there for a homeowner who wants to register (or rename) a device explicitly, e.g. to give it a nicer name before anything else references it. "front-door" is pre-registered by default, so a deployment that never touches this feature sees the exact same single device it always implicitly had.

A pass can now specify which device(s) its check-in should correlate against via deviceIds: string[] — omit it and a pass behaves exactly as before, correlating only against "front-door". POST /ring/events accepts an event for any device id, registering it on the way in.

# Register a device explicitly (optional — it would also be registered implicitly
# the first time a pass or event referenced "back-door")
curl -X POST localhost:4444/devices -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id": "back-door", "name": "Back Door"}'
curl localhost:4444/devices   # -> front-door (pre-registered) + back-door

# Issue a pass scoped to the back door only
curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Gardener", "visitorPhone": "+15551230000",
  "validUntil": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z", "deviceIds": ["back-door"]
}'
# A front-door ding will NOT correlate with this pass's check-in; a back-door ding will.

docs.title: 2. Outbound webhook notifications
docs.text:
GET /events/stream (the SSE feed) is a pull model — a client has to hold a connection open. This adds the push counterpart: a homeowner registers their own callback URL (POST /settings/webhook { "url": "..." }), and PorchPass POSTs a signed payload to it whenever a pass is issued, a visit happens, or a pass is revoked or expires — the same four event types the SSE stream emits. Signing mirrors the inbound Ring webhook verification exactly, just in the opposite direction: PorchPass generates a per-registration secret (returned once at registration, and again from GET /settings/webhook so the homeowner's receiving endpoint can be configured to verify it), computes an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw JSON body it's about to send using webhookAuth.ts's same signPayload helper, and sends it as X-PorchPass-Signature. The receiver verifies it exactly like ring/events's handler does for inbound Ring calls — recompute the same HMAC over the exact raw bytes received and compare.

Delivery retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff (~300ms, then ~600ms) on a non-2xx response or network error, and is genuinely fire-and-forget: outboundWebhooks.ts subscribes to the same eventBus passService.ts already publishes to, and never awaits the delivery — the request that triggered the event (issuing a pass, checking a visitor in, ...) returns to its caller immediately, regardless of how slow or broken the homeowner's endpoint is. Failures (and successes) are still observable: GET /settings/webhook reports the last delivery's outcome (lastSuccessAt, lastError, consecutiveFailures, ...) instead of that information disappearing into a server log no one's watching.

# Register a callback (any local HTTP listener works for testing)
curl -X POST localhost:4444/settings/webhook -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url": "https://your-backend.example/porchpass-webhook"}'
# -> { "url": "...", "secret": "<hex secret — save this>", "createdAt": "..." }

curl localhost:4444/settings/webhook   # re-fetch the secret + last delivery status any time

# On the receiving end (Node, mirroring webhookAuth.ts's verifySignature):
node -e '
  const crypto = require("node:crypto");
  const secret = "<the secret from above>";
  const rawBody = "<the exact raw request body bytes your endpoint received>";
  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
  console.log(expected === "<the X-PorchPass-Signature header value>");
'

docs.title: 3. Bulk/template pass issuance
docs.text:
POST /passes/bulk issues many passes from one call: a shared template (fields common to every pass — e.g. visitorPhone, validUntil, note) plus a variations array of per-pass overrides (a different visitorName and recurrence per weekday, or the same visitor across a list of explicit date windows). Each variation is merged onto the template and passed straight through to the existing issuePass — no separate issuance code path, so idempotency, recurrence validation, device registration, notifications, and event-bus publishing all work exactly as they do for a single POST /passes. An optional idempotencyKeyPrefix gives each item a stable, distinct idempotency key (`${idempotencyKeyPrefix}${index}`) so retrying the whole bulk call is safe too.

The response lists one result per input item — "created", "replayed" (an idempotency-key collision), or "error" (e.g. a variation missing a required field after merging) — so one bad entry doesn't sink the rest of the batch.

curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes/bulk -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "template": { "visitorPhone": "+15556660000", "validUntil": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z", "note": "weekly dog walker" },
  "variations": [
    { "visitorName": "Monday Walker",    "recurrence": { "daysOfWeek": [1], "startTime": "13:00", "endTime": "15:00" } },
    { "visitorName": "Wednesday Walker", "recurrence": { "daysOfWeek": [3], "startTime": "13:00", "endTime": "15:00" } },
    { "visitorName": "Friday Walker",    "recurrence": { "daysOfWeek": [5], "startTime": "13:00", "endTime": "15:00" } }
  ],
  "idempotencyKeyPrefix": "bulk-walkers-week1-"
}'
# -> { "results": [ { "index": 0, "status": "created", "pass": {...} }, ... ] }

docs.title: 4. Grace-period extension flow
docs.text:
A visitor who taps the check-in link moments after their pass expired used to get a flat rejection. Now, a pass that expired within the last 30 minutes (GRACE_REQUEST_WINDOW_MS in passService.ts) is flagged graceEligible: true in the check-in response instead — the visitor-facing HTML page renders a "Request a few more minutes" button, or a JSON client can call POST /checkin/:token/request-extension directly. That creates a "pending" extension request on the pass and notifies the homeowner via the existing Notifier (no new notification channel). The homeowner then approves (POST /passes/:id/extension/approve) or denies (POST /passes/:id/extension/deny) it; only approval unlocks anything, and only for 15 more minutes (EXTENSION_USABLE_WINDOW_MS) and exactly one more check-in — after that single use (or once the 15 minutes lapse unused), the pass is back to being flatly rejected, and a pass can only ever ask for one extension (a denied or never-requested pass has no second chance to ask again).

# Visitor taps the link on an expired pass -> response includes "graceEligible": true
curl -X POST localhost:4444/checkin/<token> -H "Accept: application/json"

# Visitor requests a few more minutes
curl -X POST localhost:4444/checkin/<token>/request-extension -H "Accept: application/json"
# -> homeowner is notified via the existing Notifier

# Homeowner approves (or: .../extension/deny)
curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes/<passId>/extension/approve
# -> visitor is SMS'd a link; the very next check-in within 15 minutes succeeds, then the extension is spent

docs.title: Round 4 additions
docs.text: Four more additions: visit duration tracking, a traffic/analytics report, household member roles, and encrypted-at-rest visitor PII.

docs.title: 1. Visit duration tracking
docs.text:
A "visit" used to be a single instant — the moment a visitor tapped the check-in link. Now it's a pair: an arrival (the existing POST /checkin/:token, unchanged) and, once the visitor taps "I'm leaving," a departure (POST /checkin/:token/checkout). This is a separate token action, not a direction field folded into the existing check-in endpoint — arrival already carries meaning specific to arriving (correlating a Ring event, consuming a pass's use-count, enforcing quiet hours/recurrence/expiry) that a departure has no reason to re-run; a visitor leaving doesn't need to pass the same gauntlet of validity checks that let them in, they just need to mark that they left. Checkout finds the most recently opened visit for that pass that hasn't already been checked out of and closes it, computing durationMs once at that moment. GET /visits now shows a status of "on_site" (with a live onSiteForMs) for a visit with only an arrival, or "completed" (with the final durationMs) once a departure closes it. A checkout with nothing open to close — no matching arrival at all, or a repeat call after already checking out — is rejected with a clear reason instead of silently doing nothing or crashing (see FRICTION_LOG.md for that edge case).

# Visitor arrives (as before)
curl -X POST localhost:4444/checkin/<token> -H "Accept: application/json"
# -> { "ok": true, "visit": { "id": "...", "checkedInAt": "...", ... } }

# ...later, visitor leaves
curl -X POST localhost:4444/checkin/<token>/checkout -H "Accept: application/json"
# -> { "ok": true, "visit": { "checkedOutAt": "...", "durationMs": 734000, ... } }

curl localhost:4444/visits
# -> each visit now carries "status": "on_site" | "completed", and a completed one carries "durationMs"

docs.title: 2. Traffic/analytics report
docs.text:
GET /analytics (aliased at GET /reports/traffic — both return the identical report) aggregates real visit history into plain-language insights, in the same spirit as the "StoreWatch" idea documented in hackathon-ideas/ring.md ("Tuesdays 2–4pm are your busiest window" rather than a raw event log) — folded directly into PorchPass's own visit data instead of a separate project. It reports the busiest day and hour (by arrival time, UTC), the average duration of completed visits, a count of visits per visitor and per pass note category (e.g. "dog walker" vs. "delivery" — joined from each visit's pass), how many visitors are currently on-site, and an insights array of ready-to-display sentences built from those same numbers. There's no separate analytics data store to keep in sync — every number comes straight from store.ts's existing Visit records, so the report is always as current as the last check-in or checkout.

curl localhost:4444/analytics
# -> {
#   "totalVisits": 12, "completedVisits": 9, "onSiteNow": 3,
#   "busiestDay": { "day": "Tuesday", "count": 5 },
#   "busiestHour": { "hourUtc": 14, "label": "2 PM", "count": 4 },
#   "averageVisitDurationMs": 1080000,
#   "visitsByVisitor": [ { "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker", "count": 4 }, ... ],
#   "visitsByCategory": [ { "category": "dog walker", "count": 5 }, { "category": "delivery", "count": 3 }, ... ],
#   "insights": [
#     "Tuesday is your busiest day (5 visits).",
#     "Most visits happen around 2 PM UTC (4 visits).",
#     "The average completed visit lasts 18 minutes.",
#     "\"dog walker\" is your most common visit type (5 visits).",
#     "3 visitors are currently on-site."
#   ]
# }

docs.title: 3. Household member roles
docs.text:
More than one homeowner/admin can now exist per household, with different permission levels: owner can revoke passes, approve/deny grace-period extensions, and manage household settings/webhooks; member can issue and view passes but not any of those owner-scoped actions. This is deliberately the simplest thing that demonstrates real authorization scoping without inventing a full auth system: there's no login, password, or session — a caller identifies themselves with a plain X-PorchPass-Member header (or ?member=, so a browser/curl GET can supply one too) naming a registered member id in the household directory (household.ts). This is illustrative authorization, not real authentication — a caller-supplied header proves nothing about who's actually holding the phone that sent it; a real deployment needs actual authenticated sessions (each member signs in; the server reads their identity off a verified session/JWT, never a client-supplied header). See household.ts's doc comment and FRICTION_LOG.md for the honest version of this tradeoff.

A caller who supplies no member header at all resolves to a pre-seeded default "owner" — which is what keeps every endpoint and every test from every earlier round working completely unchanged, since nothing before this round had any notion of a "caller" to begin with. An unrecognized member id is a hard 401, not a silent fallback to the lowest privilege; a recognized id with the wrong role is a 403.

# See the household's members (starts with just the pre-seeded owner)
curl localhost:4444/household/members

# The default owner adds a member-role household member (no header needed — no header = owner)
curl -X POST localhost:4444/household/members -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id": "jamie", "name": "Jamie", "role": "member"}'

# Jamie (a member) tries to revoke a pass -> 403
curl -X DELETE localhost:4444/passes/<passId> -H "X-PorchPass-Member: jamie"

# The owner revokes it instead -> 200
curl -X DELETE localhost:4444/passes/<passId> -H "X-PorchPass-Member: owner"

docs.title: 4. Encrypted-at-rest visitor PII
docs.text:
A visitor's phone number is now encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM, crypto.ts) — the in-memory Pass record stores an EncryptedField ({ iv, authTag, ciphertext }, all hex), never the plaintext number, and it's decrypted only at the one moment it's actually needed: sending the visitor's SMS (on issuance, and on an approved grace-period extension). The API itself never re-exposes the full number either — POST /passes/GET /passes return a masked visitorPhone (e.g. "••••••••1234") so a homeowner can still recognize which visitor a pass belongs to without the wire response carrying the plaintext value back out. This is illustrative, not production key management: the encryption key is derived (via scrypt, meant for passwords, not real key derivation) from PORCHPASS_ENCRYPTION_KEY, or a clearly-marked local-dev default if unset — good enough that the demo and test suite encrypt/decrypt correctly with zero configuration, and nowhere near what a real deployment should do. A real deployment must pull its data-encryption key from a proper KMS (AWS KMS, etc.), ideally via envelope encryption — see FRICTION_LOG.md for what that gap actually costs a from-scratch hackathon build.

# Issue a pass — the response's visitorPhone is masked, not the plaintext you sent.
curl -X POST localhost:4444/passes -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "visitorName": "Alex the Dog Walker", "visitorPhone": "+15551234567",
  "validUntil": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"
}'
# -> { ..., "visitorPhone": "••••••••4567", ... }
# Meanwhile the console log for the (simulated) SMS send still shows the real
# number — decrypted right there, at the point of actually sending it.

docs.title: Swapping in the real Ring API
docs.text:
Everything in src/passService.ts and src/server.ts is Ring-agnostic — it only depends on the RingClient interface (getRecentEvents, emitEvent) in src/ringClient.ts. To go from simulator to production:

  1. Implement RingClient against Ring's OAuth-authenticated device API (see the ring-api-helloworld starter sample) instead of SimulatedRingClient.
  2. Replace the payload parsing in the POST /ring/events route in server.ts with Ring's actual webhook payload shape, then append it to the same event log getRecentEvents reads from. The signature-verification wrapper around it (webhookAuth.ts) is written to mirror real webhook authentication and should carry over unchanged — just point RING_WEBHOOK_SECRET at the real shared secret Ring issues.
  3. Swap LoggingNotifier for a real SMS provider (Twilio) and/or push provider.

No change to the access-control logic itself (issuing, correlating, expiring, revoking passes) is needed — that was the point of isolating Ring behind an interface from the start.

docs.title: Judging-criteria alignment
docs.text:
• Tech Implementation: Ring event correlation (doorbell/motion → snapshot) and camera-adjacent data are treated as first-class integration points, isolated behind a RingClient interface exactly where the hackathon rules allow a simulator — the swap to Ring's real API is a one-file change, not a rewrite. The advanced round adds production-grade concerns that a hackathon demo usually skips entirely: HMAC-verified webhook ingress, an idempotency-safe write path, a real-time SSE push layer, and a rate limiter guarding the one intentionally unauthenticated endpoint. Round 3 adds the symmetric outbound half of that webhook story (signed, retried, non-blocking delivery) and generalizes the whole system from one hardcoded device to a real multi-device correlation model. Round 4 adds authorization scoping (owner vs. member roles) and encryption-at-rest for visitor PII — the two production concerns a real access-control service can't ship without, alongside turning raw visit history into an actual analytics report instead of just a log.
  • Design: A genuine "two-tap" flow — the homeowner issues a pass in one call, the visitor confirms with one tap and no app, account, or login. Passes fail closed (expired/revoked/used-up all deny access) rather than open, and now compose multiple independent policy layers cleanly (base validity → recurrence window → quiet hours → grace-period extension) rather than tangling them into one conditional. The extension flow specifically turns a hard failure mode ("you were 90 seconds late, tough luck") into a graceful, homeowner-approved recovery path instead of just a bigger grace window applied blindly to everyone.
  • Potential Impact: Solves a real, everyday problem (dog walkers, deliveries, contractors, short-term rentals) that today gets solved insecurely (a shared permanent code) or not at all (no delegated access at all). Recurring passes remove the friction of re-issuing a pass every week for a standing visitor; bulk/template issuance removes the friction of doing that by hand one pass at a time, which is what would actually make this usable for a household managing several standing visitors rather than just one. The traffic/analytics report turns a household's own visit history into the kind of operational insight the "StoreWatch" idea in hackathon-ideas/ring.md proposes for small businesses — real value for a household with several standing visitors, not just a security log nobody reads.
  • Quality of Idea: Goes beyond a notification app by adding a genuine access-delegation layer — time-boxing, use-limits, revocation, and an audit trail — on top of Ring's event stream, one of the five explicitly prioritized Ring categories ("access control"). Multi-device support and outbound webhooks both point at the same underlying idea: a household's real security setup usually has more than one camera and more than one place it wants to be told about events, and both features generalize a single-instance assumption baked into earlier rounds rather than bolting on something unrelated. A real household also usually has more than one adult with access-control authority (round 4's owner/member roles) and cares that a visitor's phone number isn't sitting in plaintext in whatever store PorchPass runs on (round 4's encryption-at-rest) — both are the kind of detail a demo can skip and a real deployment can't.

docs.title: StudyLoop (Bee)
docs.text:
Source of truth

This page mirrors bee-studyloop/README.md in the repo — edit it there, not here. Links below point back to the repo on GitHub.

docs.title: StudyLoop — Ambient Study Session Coach for Bee
docs.text:
Implementation of the "StudyLoop" idea from hackathon-ideas/bee.md: students lose track of what they actually discussed or decided in a study session, and converting ambient conversation into structured review material is friction they mostly skip. StudyLoop takes a study session's transcript, turns it into a short summary plus a set of spaced-repetition flashcards automatically, and schedules them into a daily review queue — no manual note-taking required.

Built for the Bee track of the Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon, which requires data from a real Bee wearable (or an Apple Watch running Bee software) and guides teams to integrate Bee's CLI, MCP server, or Agent Skills, prioritizing education, developer experience, and productivity.

docs.title: Scope of this submission
docs.text: This environment has no physical Bee device or Apple Watch, so this repo implements the backend service that would sit behind Bee's ambient capture — the part of StudyLoop that is genuinely testable headlessly: ingesting transcript segments, generating flashcards/summaries from them, and running the spaced-repetition scheduler that decides what to review and when. That pipeline is real, tested, and independent of where the transcript came from.

docs.title: What stands in for Bee, and what a real integration looks like
docs.text:
POST /sessions accepts a raw transcript directly (a text block, or an array of {speaker, text, timestampMs} segments) — standing in for what Bee's MCP server or CLI would hand off after a study session ends. That normalization is isolated in one function, normalizeTranscript in src/studyService.ts, which is explicitly documented as the integration seam:

  • Today: a caller (a script, a curl command, a UI) posts a transcript straight to POST /sessions.
  • With real Bee integration: instead of a human/UI posting a transcript, a small sync job would call Bee's transcript-retrieval MCP tool (e.g. a get_transcript-style tool for a session or time range) — which already returns diarized, timestamped segments in the same {speaker, text, timestampMs} shape defined in src/types.ts — and pass that array straight into normalizeTranscript/ingestSession. The array branch of normalizeTranscript is the real integration path already; only the string-splitting branch (a convenience for pasting raw text by hand, used here so the API is testable without Bee) would become dead code.
  • Nothing in flashcardGenerator.ts, scheduler.ts, studyService.ts, or server.ts needs to change to wire in the real source — they only ever see TranscriptSegment[].

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Ingest a session (POST /sessions) — post a transcript (string or segments). StudyLoop normalizes it, generates a summary and a set of flashcards, and stores them.
  2. Generate flashcards/summary — src/flashcardGenerator.ts defines an LLM-shaped FlashcardGenerator interface and ships TemplateFlashcardGenerator, a heuristic implementation with no model dependency: it pairs question/answer exchanges, extracts definition-style statements ("X is/means/refers to Y"), and falls back to cloze-deletion cards from the longest sentences so a session with neither still yields review material.
  3. Schedule review — each flashcard gets spaced-repetition state (interval, ease factor, repetitions, due date) from a simplified SM-2 algorithm in src/scheduler.ts, as pure functions.
  4. Review daily (GET /review/due) — the flashcards due today, across every session, oldest-due first.
  5. Submit a grade (POST /review/:cardId) — again / hard / good / easy; the scheduler reschedules the card's next due date and returns its updated interval/ease factor.

A second pass added six more production-grade pieces on top of that pipeline — idempotent retries, leech detection, topic tagging + search, adaptive review ordering, incremental/streaming ingestion, and a portable export — each described in detail in Advanced features below.

                           grade -> empty transcript -> raw-text transcript) plus every feature in
                           "Advanced features" and "Round 3" below, and direct unit checks of scheduler.ts,
                           leech.ts, priority.ts, and topics.ts

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
npm install
npm run build
npm start
# StudyLoop listening on http://localhost:4466

Or for local iteration: npm run dev

docs.title: Try it by hand
docs.text:
# 1. Ingest a study session transcript (stands in for a Bee ambient capture pull)
curl -X POST localhost:4466/sessions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "title": "Bio 101 study group",
  "transcript": [
    {"speaker": "Alice", "text": "Mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell."},
    {"speaker": "Bob", "text": "What is the powerhouse of the cell?"},
    {"speaker": "Alice", "text": "The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell."}
  ]
}'
# -> note the session id and the generated flashcard ids in the response

# 2. See the session's summary and flashcards again
curl localhost:4466/sessions/<sessionId>

# 3. Check today's review queue (freshly generated cards are due immediately)
curl localhost:4466/review/due

# 4. Submit a recall grade for a card ("again" | "hard" | "good" | "easy")
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "good"}'
# -> the response shows the new interval/dueAt; review again with "again" to see it drop back down

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
npm test

Starts the server on an ephemeral port and drives it over real HTTP requests: ingesting a transcript produces a non-empty summary and at least one flashcard; a fresh card appears in GET /review/due; a good grade grows its interval and moves it out of today's queue; consecutive good grades keep growing the interval; an again grade resets the streak and shortens the interval back down instead of continuing to grow it; reviewing an unknown card id or fetching an unknown session id returns a clean 404; an invalid grade returns a 400; an empty/whitespace-only transcript still returns a sensible response (a fallback summary, zero flashcards) instead of crashing; and a raw text-block transcript (not pre-segmented) is ingested successfully too. A couple of direct unit-style checks of scheduler.ts's interval/ease-factor math round it out. Every feature in Advanced features and Round 3 below has its own passing HTTP-level check plus, where the logic is pure, a direct unit-style check — see the "Feature N" tests in test/smoke.test.ts.

docs.title: Advanced features
docs.text: A second implementation pass added six production-grade features on top of the v1 pipeline above. Each is independently tested in test/smoke.test.ts (search for "Feature 1" through "Feature 6").

docs.title: 1. Idempotent session ingestion
docs.text:
POST /sessions accepts an optional idempotencyKey (or externalSessionId, treated as an alias — pass whichever you have). Re-posting the same transcript with the same key returns the original session and flashcards — same ids, no regeneration — instead of creating a duplicate study set. This is what makes a retried upload (a flaky connection, an at-least-once sync queue, a doubled tap on "sync now" in a companion app) safe to replay. The mapping from key -> session id lives in store.ts; studyService.ingestSession checks it before doing any generation work at all.

curl -X POST localhost:4466/sessions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "title": "Bio 101 study group",
  "idempotencyKey": "sync-job-run-482",
  "transcript": "Osmosis is the movement of water across a semipermeable membrane."
}'
# Re-run the exact same request (same idempotencyKey) any number of times —
# the response always has the same session.id and flashcard ids, never a duplicate.

docs.title: 2. Leech detection
docs.text:
Every flashcard tracks consecutiveFailures (consecutive "again" grades) and isLeech (true once that streak hits LEECH_THRESHOLD, currently 3 — see leech.ts). A single subsequent "good" or "easy" grade clears the flag and resets the streak; a "hard" grade neither advances nor resets it (it's a lukewarm pass, not a failure). Leeches are surfaced on their own endpoint, GET /review/leeches, distinct from the general due queue, so a student can see which cards need to be reformulated rather than endlessly rescheduled — SM-2's core blind spot.

# Grade the same card "again" three times in a row...
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "again"}'
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "again"}'
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "again"}'
# -> the response now has "isLeech": true, "consecutiveFailures": 3

curl localhost:4466/review/leeches
# -> a list of every currently-flagged leech, across every session

curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "good"}'
# -> "isLeech": false, "consecutiveFailures": 0 — one solid recall clears it

docs.title: 3. Topic tagging + search
docs.text:
When a session is ingested (or extended — see Feature 5), topics.ts extracts 1-3 heuristic topic tags from the full transcript and attaches them to every flashcard generated at that point. This is explicitly a heuristic, not real NLP or topic modeling: it scores each content word (length >= 4, not a stopword) by raw frequency, with a small bonus for words that appeared capitalized in the original text (a cheap proxy for proper nouns/key terms), and returns the top-scoring 1-3 as lowercase tags. It reliably picks out the term a session was about ("ribosome," "mitochondria") when that term is repeated, and does nothing cleverer than that. GET /flashcards/search?topic= then finds every flashcard across every session carrying a given tag, so a student can pull together material on the same topic even when it came from separate study sessions weeks apart.

curl "localhost:4466/flashcards/search?topic=ribosome"
# -> every flashcard, from any session, whose extracted topics include "ribosome"

docs.title: 4. Adaptive review ordering
docs.text:
GET /review/due no longer returns cards in plain due-date order — it ranks them by a priority score (see priority.ts, doc-commented in full there):

score = overdueDays * OVERDUE_WEIGHT           (OVERDUE_WEIGHT = 1)
      + (isLeech ? LEECH_BONUS : 0)            (LEECH_BONUS   = 10)
      + max(0, BASELINE_EASE - easeFactor)      (BASELINE_EASE = 2.5)
        * EASE_WEIGHT                           (EASE_WEIGHT   = 2)

overdueDays rewards cards that have been put off longer; the leech bonus is a large flat addition (worth ~10 days of plain overdue-ness) so a leech surfaces near the top of the queue almost regardless of its due date, because the whole point of leech-flagging is forcing it in front of the student instead of letting it get quietly rescheduled forever; the ease term gives a smaller boost to cards that have historically been hard to recall (a below-baseline SM-2 ease factor), since that's a real but softer signal than 3-in-a-row failures. Cards that aren't due yet are still filtered out first — this only reorders the pool that's already eligible today.

curl localhost:4466/review/due
# -> due cards sorted by priority score descending: a leech, or a badly overdue/hard card, first

docs.title: 5. Streaming/incremental ingestion
docs.text:
PATCH /sessions/:id/segments appends newly-captured transcript segments to an already-ingested session — the same shape POST /sessions accepts (a string, or an array of {speaker, text, timestampMs} segments) — mirroring Bee's continuous ambient capture (many small updates over the course of a session) rather than one big batch upload after the fact. It regenerates the session's summary and topic tags from the full updated transcript, but only persists flashcards that weren't already generated for this session (deduped by front text), so re-running the generator over the combined transcript doesn't re-mint duplicates for material it already produced a card from earlier.

curl -X PATCH localhost:4466/sessions/<sessionId>/segments -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "segments": [
    {"speaker": "Alice", "text": "Active transport moves molecules against a concentration gradient using energy."},
    {"speaker": "Bob", "text": "What is active transport?"},
    {"speaker": "Alice", "text": "It requires ATP to move against the gradient."}
  ]
}'
# -> { "session": { ...updated summary/segments/topics... }, "newFlashcards": [ ...only the new cards... ] }

docs.title: 6. Portable export
docs.text:
GET /sessions/:id/export (one session) and GET /export (every session) return every flashcard as a flat TSV — tab-separated rather than comma-separated because flashcard text routinely contains commas, which would otherwise need quoting. Three columns, with a header row: front, back, tags (space-separated, matching Anki's own multi-value tag convention).

curl localhost:4466/sessions/<sessionId>/export
# front back    tags
# What is a ribosome?   Ribosome function is essential for protein synthesis.   ribosome protein
# ...

To import into Anki: File -> Import, set "Fields separated by" to Tab, map column 1 -> Front, column 2 -> Back, column 3 -> Tags, and tell it to skip the header line.

docs.title: Swapping in a real LLM-backed generator
docs.text:
Everything in server.ts and studyService.ts depends only on the FlashcardGenerator interface in flashcardGenerator.ts (generate(segments) -> {summary, flashcards}), not on TemplateFlashcardGenerator specifically. To go from heuristic to model-backed:

  1. Implement FlashcardGenerator with a class that sends the segments to a model — e.g. Amazon Bedrock (natural pairing with the hackathon's AWS Builder mini-challenge) — with a prompt like "extract key facts and Q&A pairs from this study session transcript and return JSON {summary, flashcards: [{front, back}]}", then parses and validates the model's JSON response into that same shape.
  2. Swap the generator instance constructed in src/index.ts (and in tests, if desired) from new TemplateFlashcardGenerator() to new LlmFlashcardGenerator(bedrockClient).

No change to studyService.ts, scheduler.ts, or server.ts is needed — that's the point of isolating generation behind an interface from the start.

docs.title: Judging-criteria alignment
docs.text:
• Tech Implementation: The three real seams a production build would need — Bee transcript ingestion, LLM-backed generation, and spaced-repetition scheduling — are each isolated behind a small interface (normalizeTranscript's segment shape, FlashcardGenerator, and pure functions in scheduler.ts), so swapping the heuristic generator for Bedrock or wiring in Bee's real MCP tool is a scoped, single-file change, not a rewrite. The scheduler itself implements real SM-2 mechanics (interval growth, ease factor, repetition streak reset on failure), not a placeholder. The advanced round adds real production concerns on top: idempotent ingestion (safe retries), a leech-detection state machine, a documented multi-signal priority formula for review ordering, incremental ingestion that dedupes against already-generated material, and a portable export format — each isolated in its own small module (leech.ts, priority.ts, topics.ts, export.ts) and covered by its own passing test, not bolted on as a demo-only stub.
  • Design: Zero manual note-taking — a transcript in, a summary and review-ready flashcards out. The daily review surface (GET /review/due) is a single endpoint by design, matching the idea's "clean daily review flow" goal; a companion app would render it directly with no extra aggregation logic needed.
  • Potential Impact: Directly hits "education," one of the Bee track's three explicitly prioritized categories, with an everyday, recurring use case (students studying together, or half-remembering a lecture) rather than a one-off demo scenario.
  • Quality of Idea: Goes beyond a transcript viewer or generic summarizer by closing the loop into an active learning system — extraction feeding a real scheduling algorithm that adapts to how well material was recalled, which is what makes it a study coach rather than a note-taking tool.

docs.title: Round 3: quiz mode, shared decks, reminders, adaptive generation bias
docs.text: A third pass added four more features, each independently tested in test/smoke.test.ts (search for "Feature 7" through "Feature 10").

docs.title: 7. Shared study-group decks
docs.text:
POST /sessions accepts an optional shared: true, marking the resulting session as a shared study-group deck. Another student — identified by nothing more than a caller-supplied studentId string, no auth for this demo — can then call POST /decks/:sessionId/join to pull that session's flashcards into their own personal review queue. Critically, the flashcard content (front/back/tags) is never copied or regenerated: only a fresh, independent review-state row (interval, ease factor, repetitions, due date, leech tracking) is created per (studentId, card) pair. Two students who join the same deck and review the same card end up with completely independent ease factors, due dates, and leech flags — one can leech a card while the other aces it, and neither touches the card's own embedded (student-less) state, which is what every original, studentId-less endpoint still reads and writes. GET /review/due, GET /review/leeches, and POST /review/:cardId all accept an optional studentId (query param for the GETs, body field for the POST) to operate on that student's own state instead of the shared default.

# Ingest a shared deck
curl -X POST localhost:4466/sessions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "title": "Bio 101 study group", "shared": true,
  "transcript": "Meiosis is the process of cell division that produces gametes."
}'
# -> note the session id

# Two different students join the same deck
curl -X POST localhost:4466/decks/<sessionId>/join -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"studentId": "alice"}'
curl -X POST localhost:4466/decks/<sessionId>/join -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"studentId": "bob"}'

# They review the same card independently
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "easy", "studentId": "alice"}'
curl -X POST localhost:4466/review/<cardId> -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"grade": "again", "studentId": "bob"}'
# -> alice's and bob's responses show different easeFactor/dueAt/isLeech on the *same* cardId

curl "localhost:4466/review/due?studentId=alice"   # alice's own due queue
curl "localhost:4466/review/leeches?studentId=bob" # bob's own leeches

docs.title: 8. Quiz/practice-test mode
docs.text:
POST /quiz/start { count, studentId? } samples up to count cards into a new timed quiz. Sampling reuses the exact same due-filtering (isDue) and priority-ranking (priorityScore/sortByPriority) logic GET /review/due is built on — due cards come first, worst-priority (leeches, overdue, historically-hard cards) first, then, if count isn't filled, padded out with not-yet-due cards in the same priority order — rather than a separate, duplicated sampling algorithm. An optional studentId samples from that student's own personal deck (joined shared decks + directly-reviewed cards, see Feature 7) instead of the shared default pool. The response exposes each sampled card's front only — back is withheld until it's graded.

POST /quiz/:id/answer { cardId, answer } grades the response. Grading approach: a simple case-insensitive, whitespace-trimmed exact match against the card's back text (both sides lowercased, trimmed, and whitespace-collapsed before comparing) — no fuzzy matching, synonym handling, or partial credit. This is deliberately the simplest thing that could work; see FRICTION_LOG.md for the tradeoff.

GET /quiz/:id/results returns a score summary — usable mid-quiz (a partial score) or once every sampled card has been answered (complete: true) — including exactly which cards were missed, with their prompt/answer, so a student can review what they got wrong right after finishing.

curl -X POST localhost:4466/quiz/start -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"count": 5, "studentId": "alice"}'
# -> { "id": "...", "cards": [ { "cardId": "...", "front": "What is meiosis?" }, ... ] }

curl -X POST localhost:4466/quiz/<quizId>/answer -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "cardId": "<cardId>", "answer": "a process of cell division that produces gametes"
}'
# -> { "correct": true } or { "correct": false }

curl localhost:4466/quiz/<quizId>/results
# -> { "total": 5, "answered": 3, "correct": 2, "complete": false, "missed": [ {"cardId": "...", "front": "...", "back": "...", "submittedAnswer": "..."} ] }

docs.title: 9. Due-card reminder digest
docs.text:
GET /reminders/digest?studentId= returns a compact, single-paragraph summary of that student's own due queue — built from the exact same per-student due/leech logic Features 7 and 8 use, so it can't drift out of sync with what the student would actually see — designed to be easy for another service or a voice assistant to read aloud directly, e.g. "You have 5 cards due today, including 2 leeches." The response also includes the structured counts the sentence is built from (due, dueLeeches, totalLeeches, totalCards), for a caller that wants to render its own UI instead of just reading the sentence.

curl "localhost:4466/reminders/digest?studentId=alice"
# -> {
#      "studentId": "alice",
#      "summary": "You have 5 cards due today, including 2 leeches.",
#      "counts": { "due": 5, "dueLeeches": 2, "totalLeeches": 3, "totalCards": 12 }
#    }

docs.title: 10. Adaptive new-card generation bias
docs.text:
PATCH /sessions/:id/segments now accepts an optional studentId. When given, appending new material biases flashcard generation toward topics that student has historically struggled with. The exact heuristic:

  1. A topic (one of a card's heuristic tags, see Feature 3 in the previous round) counts as weak for a student if, across every card of theirs (joined or directly reviewed) carrying that tag, the average ease factor is below 2.0 (meaningfully under scheduler.ts's 2.5 baseline) — or at least one of those cards is currently flagged a leech. A leech alone is enough regardless of average ease, since three failures in a row is a stronger signal than a merely-below-average ease factor (the same priority priority.ts already gives leeches over ease elsewhere).
  2. The topics of just the newly appended segments (not the full transcript) are extracted the same way any other ingest does (topics.ts).
  3. If any of those overlap the student's weak topics, up to 3 extra simple cloze-deletion cards (fill-in-the- blank, blanking the longest word in each new sentence) are generated from the new segments alone and added on top of whatever the generator's normal Q&A/definition/cloze tiers already produced for the full transcript — so a weak topic visibly yields more review material than a topic the student is already acing, which produces nothing extra.
# alice previously failed several "photosynthesis"-tagged cards -> that topic is now "weak" for her
curl -X PATCH localhost:4466/sessions/<sessionId>/segments -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "studentId": "alice",
  "segments": "Photosynthesis also depends on chlorophyll concentration in the leaf."
}'
# -> "newFlashcards" includes both whatever the normal tiers found AND a few extra
#    "Fill in the blank: ..." cards from just this new sentence, because photosynthesis is weak for alice.
# The same PATCH with no studentId (or a studentId with no weak topics) yields only the normal-tier cards.

See FRICTION_LOG.md for this heuristic's real limitations (topic granularity, cold-start behavior, and why "more cards" rather than "simpler cards" was the chosen bias).

docs.title: Round 4: streaks & gamification, session planner, import round-trip, regenerate-a-card
docs.text: A fourth pass added four more features, each independently tested in test/smoke.test.ts (search for "Feature 11" through "Feature 14").

docs.title: 11. Study streaks & gamification
docs.text:
Every review submitted with a studentId (POST /review/:cardId { grade, studentId }) now also folds into that student's daily streak (see streak.ts). A "streak day" is any UTC calendar day on which the student completed at least one review — reviewing ten cards in one sitting only counts once. Consecutive streak days grow currentStreak; a day with zero reviews breaks it: the next review resets currentStreak back to 1 (the day it happens on still counts), but longestStreak only ever grows, never shrinks. Milestone badges (3-day-streak, 7-day-streak, 30-day-streak) are earned based on longestStreak, so once earned a badge is never revoked just because the current streak later resets — the same "permanent achievement" model most habit trackers use.

GET /students/:studentId/streak returns the current state; a student who has never reviewed anything gets a valid all-zero response rather than a 404 (asking about a streak that hasn't started isn't an error).

curl localhost:4466/students/alice/streak
# -> { "studentId": "alice", "currentStreak": 4, "longestStreak": 12, "badges": ["3-day-streak", "7-day-streak"], "lastActiveDate": "2026-03-04" }

Note: since streaks are keyed off a studentId, only reviews submitted through the shared-decks studentId path count toward one — the original, student-less "default reviewer" endpoint (POST /review/:cardId with no studentId) has no single student to credit and never touches streak state.

docs.title: 12. Global daily review session planner
docs.text:
GET /review/session?studentId=&maxCards=<n> builds one bounded "here's your review for today" session across every deck a student has — their own directly-reviewed cards and every shared deck they've joined (Feature 7) — in the exact same adaptive priority order GET /review/due already uses (priorityScore/sortByPriority), then caps the result at maxCards. This is deliberately a thin wrapper around the existing per-student due-card query, not a new ranking algorithm: the planner's job is the cap and the "how many are left for later" count (totalDue), not a different ordering. A leech or badly-overdue card from one deck still outranks a merely-due card from another, so capping never means silently dropping the most urgent material.

curl "localhost:4466/review/session?studentId=alice&maxCards=15"
# -> {
#      "studentId": "alice", "maxCards": 15, "totalDue": 42,
#      "cards": [ /* up to 15 PersonalFlashcardView objects, worst-priority first, across every deck alice has */ ]
#    }

docs.title: 13. Import round-trip
docs.text:
POST /import { tsv, sessionId?, title? } is the inverse of GET /export/GET /sessions/:id/export: it parses a TSV in that exact format (front, back, tags, header optional — see fromPortableTsv in export.ts) and creates flashcards from it, so a student can back up a deck and restore it later, or migrate cards between environments (a local dev instance and a deployed one, say). Pass sessionId to import into an existing session; omit it to create a fresh one (the "restore a full backup" shape).

Deduplication, exactly as documented: a row is skipped (counted in skippedDuplicates, not created) if its trimmed, lowercased front text matches either (a) a flashcard the target session already has, or (b) an earlier row already accepted from this same import batch. That second half matters even for a brand-new session: a TSV with an accidental duplicate row still only produces one card. Imported cards always start with fresh scheduling/leech state (interval: 0, no leech history) — a TSV export carries no review history to restore, only front/back/tags survive the round trip (see FRICTION_LOG.md).

# Back up a deck
curl localhost:4466/sessions/<sessionId>/export -o backup.tsv

# ...later, or in a different environment: restore it into a brand-new session
# (jq builds the JSON body so the TSV's tabs/newlines are escaped correctly)
jq -Rs '{tsv: .}' backup.tsv | curl -X POST localhost:4466/import -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @-
# -> { "session": {...}, "imported": [ ...new Flashcard objects... ], "skippedDuplicates": 0 }

# Re-importing the same backup into the same session is a safe no-op
jq -Rs --arg sid "<sessionId>" '{tsv: ., sessionId: $sid}' backup.tsv | curl -X POST localhost:4466/import -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @-
# -> "imported": [], "skippedDuplicates": <row count>

docs.title: 14. Regenerate-a-card
docs.text:
POST /flashcards/:cardId/regenerate re-runs flashcard generation to produce an alternative phrasing for one existing card, replacing its front/back in place. Everything else — id, tags, and every bit of spaced-repetition/leech state (interval, easeFactor, repetitions, dueAt, consecutiveFailures, isLeech) — is carried over untouched, so regenerating a confusingly-worded card doesn't cost a student their progress on it.

It reuses the same injected FlashcardGenerator every other ingestion path uses — no separate regeneration logic. The only new piece is recovering which part of the session's transcript the card came from (findUnderlyingSegments in studyService.ts), so regeneration runs the generator over just that material instead of the whole session (which would just reproduce the same card set the original ingest already did). This exploits how each generator tier builds a card's text: a Q&A card's front/back are the two source segments' text verbatim, so an exact match recovers them exactly; a cloze card's blanked word can be substituted back in to reconstruct the original sentence and locate it; a definition card only has "the segment mentioning the term" as a fallback signal, since its front is reworded rather than verbatim. If the generator's normal tiers produce nothing different for that material (a real possibility for terse source text), regeneration falls back to generateClozeCards — the same exported helper Feature 10's adaptive bias already reuses — for a guaranteed-different fill-in-the-blank phrasing, rather than writing a second cloze generator.

curl -X POST localhost:4466/flashcards/<cardId>/regenerate
# -> the same card id, with a fresh front/back and identical interval/easeFactor/dueAt/isLeech
